name: Colin Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two hundred and ten dairy cows, milked twice a day in a herringbone parlour, which is the kind where the cows stand at an angle in two rows and you work in a pit between them. First milking starts at five. I do the morning one with Rob, my son, then breakfast, then it's feeding, checking for cows on heat, and the endless business of slurry. We grow maize and grass silage on the rest of the two hundred and fifty acres.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the routine more than I'd admit. Cows are creatures of habit and so am I. What wears me out is the milk price going up and down like a yo-yo, and the five o'clock starts in January when the pipes freeze and the parlour feels like a fridge.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's on the farm with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rob's thirty-two and he's the herd manager now, really, I just think I'm in charge. We've got two milkers, Stefan and Lee. My wife Sue is a vet nurse part-time in town. Our daughter Claire does marketing for a building firm in the city.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. Rob got me using one to compare feed quotes and check the vet's notes. I don't trust it with anything important. Last month it told me a cow's due date that was three weeks out, which in my world is a big mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for quotes and that's about it. At the discussion group I'd say what I always say: show me the numbers on a real farm and I'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, and I'm fine with that. The milk price is still the milk price. AI doesn't move the pound per litre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what we're doing. Probably re-roof the old cubicle shed, which is quoted at eighteen thousand. Rob wants to look at collars that track when cows are on heat. I'd let him, once two farms in the group say they've paid for themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, honestly. Steady is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for two farms in the group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I bought a feed system in 2012 that the salesman swore would save me a fortune, and it broke every winter. Now I wait until someone I know has had it through a winter. Mike down the road is usually first, God bless him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Rob get frustrated with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Constantly. He says I'd still be milking by hand if he'd let me. We have a row about it every six months. Then he usually wins, a year later than he wanted.

S0.say: It's handy for feed quotes and that's about it. At the discussion group I'd say show me the numbers on a real farm and I'll listen.
S0.think: Nothing changes for me, and I'm fine with that. The milk price is still the milk price, and AI doesn't move the pound per litre.
S0.do: Re-roofs the old cubicle shed for a quoted eighteen thousand. Lets his son Rob try heat-detection collars on the cows once two farms in their discussion group say they've paid for themselves.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, since steady is how he likes things.
S0.quote: He says I'd still be milking by hand if he'd let me. We have a row about it every six months.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is measured and numbers-led, and his caution comes from a costly mistake in 2012. The farm runs on a friendly tug of war with his son over new kit. He is genuinely content when nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is sensible. Rushing never did farming any good. And firms hiring fewer young people is short-sighted, but I wouldn't make a big fuss about it, it's their business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow suits me fine. The tricky part is Rob. He's waiting to take over the farm, and if things change slowly, the question of when I step back gets slower too. I can see that bothering him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let Rob put the collars on the cows, which by then other farms will have tested. Probably spend around ten thousand. Sit down with Rob and the accountant and actually write down a date for handing over, maybe sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A bit uneasy about the handover talk, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the handover talk uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because once I put a date on it, it's real. My father never set a date, he just kept going until his heart gave out in the parlour. I don't want that for Rob or for me, but saying it out loud is hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Stefan and Lee? Does slow change touch them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Some of what they do, the cow records, the feed mixing, a computer might take a bit of. But someone still needs to put the clusters on. Stefan's been here twelve years. He'll see me out.

S1.say: Slow is sensible, because rushing never did farming any good. Firms hiring fewer young people is short-sighted, but I wouldn't make a big fuss.
S1.think: Slow suits me, but the tricky part is Rob, who is waiting to take over. If everything changes slowly, the question of when I step back drifts too.
S1.do: Lets Rob fit heat-detection collars, spending around ten thousand, once others have tested them. Sits down with Rob and the accountant to write down a handover date, probably at sixty-two.
S1.feel: Fairly calm, with some unease about putting a date on handing over the farm.
S1.quote: My father never set a date, he just kept going until his heart gave out in the parlour.
S1.fieldNote: The AI scenario became a conversation about succession, which is clearly what's really on his mind. His father's death in the parlour shapes his wish to plan. He is relaxed about his staff in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mess and both sides are making it worse by shouting. Help the people who lose their jobs, sure, but don't stop the companies using it either. Somewhere in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's Claire I'd think of. Marketing for a building firm is exactly the sort of office job these assistants could do. She's thirty, renting in the city, and she's never had to look for work in a downturn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Phone Claire and ask her straight what her company is doing. Tell her she can come home for a few months if she needs to, there's the cottage Stefan used to rent. Use an assistant myself for the milk contracts and the cow records, once Rob's set it up and it's been right for a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Claire. For the farm, it'd be fine. Office work isn't milking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Claire on that phone call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something unhelpful like, have you thought about the agricultural side? Marketing for feed companies or machinery firms. They still need people who can talk to farmers, and she grew up on one. She'd roll her eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use the assistant yourself. Does it bother you that it's the same kind of tool that might take Claire's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But that's how it's always been. The milking machine took jobs from people who milked by hand. You don't refuse the machine, you look after the people.

S2.say: It's a mess and both sides are making it worse by shouting. Help people who lose their jobs, but don't stop companies using it either.
S2.think: It's Claire I'd think of, because her marketing job is just the sort of office work these assistants could do. She's thirty, renting in the city, and has never job hunted in a downturn.
S2.do: Calls his daughter Claire to ask what her firm is planning and offers her the empty farm cottage. Uses an assistant for milk contracts and cow records once Rob has set it up and it's proved reliable for a few months.
S2.feel: Uneasy for his daughter, and relaxed about the farm itself.
S2.quote: The milking machine took jobs from people who milked by hand. You don't refuse the machine, you look after the people.
S2.fieldNote: His centre view is clear: accept the technology, support the people. He uses the history of his own trade to make sense of it. His worry shifts to his daughter, and he offers practical help rather than comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there needs to be a fair deal, and both parties need to stop playing games and agree one. Some tax on the big winners, but don't wreck the economy chasing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, a dairy farm with land would look very good on paper. But land prices booming doesn't help me milk cows. It makes it harder for Rob, because the tax on handing over gets bigger as the land's worth more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get proper advice on the handover, quickly, before any tax rules change. Probably three thousand on a good adviser. Keep the farm as it is otherwise. Put a bit aside for Claire if she loses her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the handover and the tax. Odd, really, because it's good news on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's good news on paper. Why doesn't it feel good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm never selling. The land's only worth something if you sell it, and I'm handing it to Rob. So all a boom does for me is make the paperwork harder and the tax bigger. It's like being told your house is worth a million when you're living in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most in the village?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young couples. If house prices boom, Lee and his girlfriend will never buy a house round here. He's twenty-nine and on milker's wages. I'd probably end up offering him the cottage too, and then where does Claire go?

S3.say: There needs to be a fair deal, and both parties need to stop playing games and agree one. Tax the big winners a bit, but don't wreck the economy chasing them.
S3.think: My land would look very good on paper, but booming prices don't help me milk cows. They make it harder for Rob, because the tax on handing over grows with the land's value.
S3.do: Pays about three thousand for proper advice on handing the farm to Rob before any tax rules change. Keeps the farm as it is and sets money aside for Claire in case she loses her job.
S3.feel: Anxious about the handover and tax, which feels odd when it's good news on paper.
S3.quote: It's like being told your house is worth a million when you're living in it.
S3.fieldNote: Rising land value worries him rather than pleasing him, because he'll never sell. Succession is the thread through every picture. He also sees the housing squeeze on his young milker, and has more people than cottages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in dairy aren't new, there are milking robots now. The question is whether the rest of the farm goes robot, and whether ordinary farms can afford it. I'd want the government to help smaller farms keep up, not leave them behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I've been looking at milking robots for five years and never pulled the trigger. If they suddenly get cheap and good, I'd probably buy them. That's the uncomfortable truth. It'd mean Stefan and Lee aren't needed for milking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Visit three farms with the new robots in the first six months, see them through a winter. Probably buy two milking robots in year two, at around a hundred and fifty thousand each. Move Stefan onto the youngstock and the robots' maintenance, and help Lee find work elsewhere, with a reference and a few months' pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Torn. Part of me is relieved for my back and for Rob's future. Part of me feels like a traitor to Stefan and Lee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him first, before anyone in the pub does. I'd tell him he's young enough to learn the robot side and I'd pay for a course. But I don't know if there'd be a job at the end of it, and I wouldn't lie to him about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Before, you said the milking machine took jobs and you look after the people. Is that what you'd be doing here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be trying. With Stefan, yes. With Lee, I'd be helping him leave, which isn't the same thing. I'd have to admit that.

S4.say: Robots in dairy aren't new, there are milking robots already. The question is whether ordinary farms can afford the rest going robot, and the government should help smaller farms keep up.
S4.think: I've looked at milking robots for five years and never bought. If they got cheap and good, I'd probably buy them, which means Stefan and Lee wouldn't be needed for milking.
S4.do: Visits three farms using the new robots over a winter in the first six months. Plans to buy two milking robots at about a hundred and fifty thousand each in year two, moves Stefan to youngstock and maintenance, and helps Lee leave with a reference and a few months' pay.
S4.feel: Torn between relief for his back and his son's future, and feeling like a traitor to his two milkers.
S4.quote: With Lee, I'd be helping him leave, which isn't the same thing. I'd have to admit that.
S4.fieldNote: Here he would be the one bringing in robots, and he knows it. When I reminded him of his milking machine line, he admitted he'd only partly be looking after people. His steady pace survives even this: he still wants to see the robots through a winter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast robots, because I'd have to choose between the farm and the men who work on it. What would help is low-interest loans so ordinary family farms can buy the kit, and a proper scheme for workers like Lee to retrain, paid partly by the robot makers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the handover. Every picture, I ended up talking about Rob taking over. For a farmer my age, that's the real question. AI or not, someone has to be standing in the parlour in ten years.

headlineQuote: AI or not, someone has to be standing in the parlour in ten years.
portrait: Colin Dubois is fifty-eight and milks two hundred and ten cows with his son Rob, who is the herd manager in all but name. He is careful and numbers-led, uses AI now and then, and waits until a neighbour has run new kit through a winter before buying. His views are firmly in the middle: help the people, don't stop the technology. In every picture his thoughts drift back to handing the farm to Rob, and to his daughter Claire's office job. In the robot picture he admits he'd probably buy milking robots himself and would be helping one of his milkers leave, not protecting him.
biggestWorry: The fast robots picture, because he would have to choose between the farm's future and the men who work on it.
whatWouldHelp: Low-interest loans so ordinary family farms can afford the new kit, and a retraining scheme for workers like Lee paid partly by the robot makers.
